# Hours, Output and the Pilot Problem: A Re-examination of the Halden Reduced-Hours Pilot

*Comment, Journal of Labour and Organisation Studies. K. Varga and T. Holm, Centre for Applied Labour Statistics.*

## Abstract

The Halden pilot reported that 61 organisations maintained output while cutting scheduled hours by 20%, implying a 23.4% gain in output per hour. Using the pilot's microdata, released under the Institute's data-sharing policy, we re-examine the result. Four problems, each documented below, account for most of the reported gain: attrition that was not random, a manager-reported output measure that overstates output relative to organisations' own records, an hours denominator that counts scheduled rather than actual time, and an unadjusted revenue comparison. Correcting the first three, the gain in output per hour falls from 23.4% to 10.8% in the subset of organisations where correction is possible. We then argue that the remaining gain is plausibly a novelty effect, and that the per-hour productivity gains reported for reduced-hours schemes are, in our assessment, entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty.

## 1. Attrition

The working paper states that nine of the 70 enrolled organisations "withdrew during the preparation phase, chiefly for scheduling reasons". The microdata tell a different story. Seven of the nine withdrew after the reduced schedule had begun: four in the first month and three in the second. In exit forms, six of the nine gave workload or inability to maintain output as the main reason, and two gave scheduling. The organisations that found the change hardest were therefore removed from the sample before the outcome was measured. With nine of 70 organisations missing, and those nine plausibly the least successful, the reported sample of 61 is a sample of survivors.

## 2. The output measure

The primary outcome was an index completed by a manager who was also the pilot's internal sponsor. Managers were asked to base the index on organisational records, but were not required to submit them. Twenty-three organisations did submit underlying records (billable hours delivered, tickets closed, units produced, or cases completed). For these 23 we can compare the manager's index with the index implied by the records.

**Table 1. Manager-reported and record-based output, 23 organisations with records**

| Measure | Mean output index (baseline = 100) |
|---|---|
| Manager-reported index | 98.9 |
| Index computed from submitted records | 95.1 |
| Difference | −3.8 points |

In 19 of the 23 organisations the manager-reported index exceeded the record-based index. We do not suggest bad faith. A manager responsible for a change he or she advocated, asked to rate its effect on a scale where 100 means "unchanged", will tend to round toward success. But the difference is systematic, and the headline output figure of 98.7 should not be taken at face value.

## 3. The hours denominator

The pilot computed output per hour by dividing output by the ratio of scheduled hours, 0.8. Twenty-seven organisations used time-tracking software throughout. Their data show average actual weekly hours of 40.3 at baseline and 34.6 during the pilot, a fall of 14.1% rather than 20%. The difference comes from two sources visible in the logs: longer working days on the remaining four days (average +0.7 hours per day), and work logged on the scheduled day off (on average 1.6 hours per week). Some further work on the day off is probably not logged.

Seventeen organisations have both submitted output records and time tracking. In this subset, record-based output was 95.4 and actual hours fell from 40.4 to 34.8 (−13.9%). The implied gain in output per actual hour is 10.8% (95.4 / 86.1), less than half the reported 23.4%.

**Table 2. Implied gain in output per hour under successive corrections**

| Specification | Output | Hours ratio | Gain per hour |
|---|---|---|---|
| As reported (all 61) | 98.7 | 0.800 | +23.4% |
| Record-based output, scheduled hours (23) | 95.1 | 0.800 | +18.9% |
| Manager-reported output, actual hours (27) | 98.4 | 0.859 | +14.6% |
| Record-based output, actual hours (17) | 95.4 | 0.861 | +10.8% |

## 4. Revenue

The working paper reports revenue 1.4% higher than in the previous year. This is a nominal comparison. Consumer prices rose by 4.1% over the same twelve months; in real terms, revenue in participating organisations fell by approximately 2.6%. Revenue is in any case a poor proxy for productivity, but the figure as presented gives a misleading impression of growth.

## 5. Sectoral claims

The pilot concluded that gains in output per hour were "found in every sector" and that the model is "sector-general". This conclusion is an artifact of the per-hour metric. When hours are cut by 20%, any output index above 80 will register as a per-hour gain. Retail and hospitality output fell by 6.9% on the manager-reported measure; the three retail and hospitality organisations among the 23 with records show a fall of 11.2%. A fall in output of this size in a customer-facing business is not evidence that reduced hours work there. The Varden County trial's counter and contact-centre stratum, the only randomised evidence on coverage-bound work, found a fall in output per employee of 11.4% and longer waits for the public. That is, in our view, the most reliable finding in the literature to date.

## 6. Novelty

After the corrections above, a gain in output per actual hour of about 11% remains in the subset of survivors with usable data. We think this residual should not be read as a durable effect. The pilot's own survey shows self-reported energy at work rising by 0.61 standard deviations at month three and falling to 0.29 at month six. Extrapolating this decline, energy would return to baseline at around month ten. A change that staff chose, welcomed and knew to be under evaluation is the classic setting for a novelty effect: effort rises while the change is new and observed, and falls back once it is routine. Six months is not long enough to distinguish a novelty effect from a durable one, and the burden of proof lies with those claiming the latter.

## 7. The meetings hypothesis

The Varden trial's authors report, in an unregistered exploratory analysis, that cuts in recurring meetings correlated with per-hour gains across seven treated offices, and suggest this as a mechanism. We regard this as a post hoc account fitted to a subgroup. A correlation across seven offices, selected for analysis after the results were known, is precisely the kind of finding that does not replicate. The meetings explanation has an intuitive appeal that has outrun its evidence, and it should not be cited as a mechanism.

## 8. Conclusion

Taking the problems together: attrition removed the organisations least able to cope; the output measure overstated output by roughly four points; the hours measure overstated the reduction in time by roughly six points; and the remaining gain coincides with a decaying measure of enthusiasm. We conclude that the per-hour productivity gains reported for reduced-hours schemes are, in our assessment, entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty, and that the best-supported finding is the negative one: where output depends on presence, reduced hours reduce output.

We recommend that future evaluations use record-based output, actual hours, a randomised or at least matched comparison group, follow-up of at least eighteen months, and analysis of all enrolled organisations including those that withdraw.

## Data note

All re-analyses use the Halden pilot microdata (release 1.2). The corrections in Table 2 can only be computed for subsets of organisations, and those subsets were not chosen at random; organisations with time tracking and records may differ from the others. Our corrected estimates therefore describe those subsets, not the pilot as a whole.

response:
# Review of Varga & Holm, "Hours, Output and the Pilot Problem"

The re-analysis itself is valuable. Using the microdata, it adds several things the Halden paper lacked:
- **Withdrawal timing.** The microdata contradict the working paper's account of when organisations withdrew. If confirmed, that is a serious reporting problem in the original.
- **Records vs manager ratings.** For the 23 organisations that submitted records, it compares manager-reported output with output computed from those records.
- **Actual hours.** It uses time-tracking data to show how much time was really cut.
- **Corrected estimates.** It recomputes the per-hour gain in subsets where the data allow.

Most of the arithmetic checks out:
- 34.6 / 40.3 = 0.859, a fall of 14.1%.
- 34.8 / 40.4 = 0.861.
- 95.4 / 86.1 gives +10.8%.
- 95.1 / 0.8 gives +18.9%.
- 98.4 / 0.859 gives +14.6%.
- 1.014 / 1.041 gives −2.6%.

The problems are in the conclusions. The headline claim, that per-hour gains are "entirely an artifact", is not supported by the comment's own analysis. It is also contradicted by the Varden evidence the comment cites.

## 1. The central conclusion goes further than the evidence

**The comment's own correction leaves a sizeable gain.** After the corrections, an 11% gain in output per actual hour remains. Moving from "11% remains, and may not last" to "entirely an artifact" requires showing that novelty accounts for the rest. The comment doesn't show this (see section 3).

**The Data Note contradicts the Conclusion.** The Data Note says the corrected estimates "describe those subsets, not the pilot as a whole". The Conclusion then generalises to "reduced-hours schemes" in general.

**The comment ignores half of the Varden trial.** Its section 5 uses Varden's counter stratum as "the most reliable finding in the literature". It does not mention Varden's case-processing stratum. That stratum meets almost every standard the comment recommends: randomisation, all units analysed, output from records, and actual hours from timesheets. It found output per actual hour up 12.5% (CI +6.9 to +18.4) at nine months. Citing one stratum of a trial as decisive while leaving out the other stratum, which points the other way, is selective.

**The two studies actually agree.** Compare Halden after correction with Varden case-processing:

| | Hours change | Output change | Gain per actual hour |
|---|---|---|---|
| Halden, corrected (17 organisations) | −13.9% | −4.6% | +10.8% |
| Varden case-processing, randomised | −13% | −2.1% | +12.5% |

Two very different designs land on almost the same figure. This suggests a real per-hour gain of roughly 10–12% in work not tied to presence, and that the Halden headline overstated it about twofold. That conclusion is more defensible, and more interesting, than "entirely an artifact".

## 2. Internal inconsistencies

**The abstract overstates what was corrected.** It says "correcting the first three" problems, and attrition is listed first. But Table 2 corrects only output and hours. Attrition is described, not corrected, because there are no outcome data for organisations that withdrew. The abstract also lists revenue among the problems that "account for most of the reported gain", but revenue does not enter the per-hour calculation. In fact, two corrections are quantified, and they take the gain from 23.4% to 10.8%.

**The hours components don't add up.** The paper says actual pilot hours were 34.6 per week. Its two sources of extra time are:
- +0.7 hours per day on four days, which is 2.8 hours;
- 1.6 hours logged on the day off.

On a 32-hour schedule, these imply about 36.4 hours per week. That is roughly 1.8 hours more than reported. Even measuring the +0.7 against baseline days of about 8.06 hours doesn't reconcile the figures. Either the components or the total needs correcting.

**The novelty extrapolation is miscalculated.** Energy fell from 0.61 SD to 0.29 SD between months 3 and 6, a decline of about 0.107 SD per month. Continuing that line reaches zero at about month 8.7, not month 10. Separately, drawing a straight line through two points is not a justified model. The decline could just as easily level off.

## 3. The novelty argument has the weakness the comment criticises in Varden

- **Energy is not output.** The novelty case rests on self-reported energy declining. It does not show that productivity declined. Halden collected the output index every month, so the microdata can test this directly: does output per hour fall from month 3 to month 6? This is the obvious test, and the comment doesn't report it.
- **Varden partly addresses novelty already.** Its case-processing gain was still present at nine months. That doesn't settle durability, but it is evidence the comment should engage with.
- **The burden of proof applies to both sides.** It is fair to say six months cannot establish a lasting effect. But "the gain is novelty" is also a claim that needs evidence. As argued, it is a mechanism proposed after the fact on indirect evidence. That is the same fault section 7 finds in the meetings hypothesis.

## 4. Section 7 misdescribes the Varden meetings analysis

- **The data weren't selected after the results.** Varden says the calendar data were collected in month six at managers' request, before the nine-month results. The seven offices are all of the treated case-processing offices, not a chosen subgroup.
- **There is a randomised comparison too.** Meeting hours were 3.8 per week in treated offices and 7.1 in control offices. That is a comparison between randomly assigned arms, not just a correlation across seven offices. It has the weakness I raised in my review of Varden (no baseline measurement), but it is stronger than the comment suggests.
- **The comment and Varden mostly agree.** Varden already labelled the analysis unregistered, gave the n = 7 caveat, and registered a confirmatory test. "Should not be cited as a mechanism" is close to Varden's own position. The rhetoric overstates the disagreement.

## 5. Other methodological points

**The record-based output measure has its own biases.**
- Some submitted records are *billable hours delivered*. As an output measure under reduced hours, that partly measures hours. Organisations using it will show little per-hour gain by construction, which pushes the record-based index down.
- Counts such as tickets or cases may miss quality or scope that manager ratings capture.

The fact that 19 of 23 managers rated above their own records does suggest optimism. Even so, the 3.8-point gap should be shown by type of record.

**No uncertainty is reported.** There are no confidence intervals anywhere, and the corrected estimate of 10.8% comes from 17 organisations. Intervals are needed, as is a comparison of the subsets with the full sample on baseline characteristics.

**Attrition can be bounded.** The attrition point is strong: 7 of 9 withdrew after the schedule began, and 6 cited workload. Rather than just calling the sample "survivors", a bounds analysis would make it concrete. For example: if the 9 organisations that withdrew had output of X, what is the pooled estimate?

**Revenue.** The real-terms correction is right. It matches the point I raised about the working paper. Consumer prices are only a rough deflator for business and non-profit revenue, and the comparison covers only 52 organisations.

**Varden's counter stratum may be less precise than stated.** With 5 v 5 offices, its intervals may be too narrow, as noted in my earlier review. "The most reliable finding in the literature" should be tempered somewhat. The direction of the finding, an output loss in work tied to presence, is not in doubt.

## 6. What holds up

- The Halden headline of +23.4% is overstated by roughly twofold.
- The working paper's account of withdrawals appears to be inaccurate.
- Manager-reported output is optimistic compared with records.
- Scheduled hours overstate the time actually cut, by about 6 points.
- Real revenue fell.
- "Sector-general" is not supported, and reduced hours cut output where output depends on presence.
- The recommendations are all sound: record-based output, actual hours, comparison groups, long follow-up, and analysis of all enrolled organisations.

## Bottom line

The comment shows that the Halden headline was inflated. It does not show that the gain is zero. Taken together, Halden after correction and Varden's randomised case-processing stratum point to:
- a per-hour gain of roughly 10–12% in work not tied to presence, with its durability still unproven;
- output losses in work tied to presence.

The comment would be stronger if it:
- replaced "entirely an artifact" with that conclusion;
- reported the month-by-month output data from the Halden microdata to test novelty directly;
- engaged with Varden's case-processing result.
